featured_reviews.name: Ramya Iyer
featured_reviews.review_text:
This is one of the most education oriented college in Mumbai. Being a BA passout, my experience was northing short of incredible. I completed both junior and degree college here. The faculty is an expert in their own subjects.

Why and how does the college stand out?
1. The faculty is too good in their field
2. There are a lot of clubs in the college, each club exposes you to something new
3. There is a seperate cloak room for the BMM department
4. A dedicated ladies common room where female students can have their respective study time, spend their free time between 2 lectures, bunk and sit here
5. A NCC cell inside the ladies common room
6. Value lab, NPTEL clubs can bring out the best in you-do check with Kamala ma'am and Mahalakshmi ma'am.
7. Don't forget to check with NCC and rotary club here-the most lively clubs
8. The education here is the best, students get to learn a lot here
9. Environment is too good
10. Washrooms are always clean and cleaned regularly
11. Prime location-both bus stop and railway stations -Sion and GTB are at a walking distance
12. The library is very extensive-wide range of educational  books and newsletters+ novels-fiction and non-fiction for all the language graduates.

featured_reviews.name: Indroneel Chatterjee
featured_reviews.review_text:
My critique comes not from resentment, but from direct experience in pedagogy and over a decade of working within universities at a senior level, which has given me the distance and analytical ability to understand just how profoundly wrong this programme was from an objective vantage point. This reflection is retrospective, yes; but that does not soften it. If anything, it clarifies it. I cannot find a silver lining.

I studied BMM (Bachelor in Mass Media) (2009–2012), and in pedagogical terms, it was a complete car crash.

From the outset, the programme suffered from institutional nepotism. The head of faculty was the vice principal’s daughter; someone with no formal background in education, curriculum design, or pedagogy. While she did have hands-on industry experience (which is not inherently problematic), leading an academic programme requires more than practical exposure. It requires an understanding of learning outcomes, assessment integrity, curriculum coherence, and academic standards. None of this was evident. The programme felt less like a degree and more like an ongoing experiment, with students as unwilling test subjects.

There was a heavy reliance on guest lecturers, which in principle can be enriching. In practice, it signalled a lack of ownership and structure. Content appeared to be patched together on a trial-and-error basis, with no clear progression, coherence, or pedagogical rationale. The course felt improvised rather than designed.

Worse still, the environment was riddled with favouritism. Boundaries between staff and students were poorly defined. Students who engaged in overt flattery were rewarded; those who didn’t were quietly sidelined. This was not subtle, and it was not accidental. Whether this reflected wider institutional practice or was specific to my cohort being the first under an inexperienced programme head is unclear; but the damage was done regardless.

The broader institutional leadership offered no corrective. The principal at the time embodied a hollow authoritarianism; strict in tone, performative in discipline, but devoid of substance or ethical leadership. One particularly absurd low point was an “Eve teasing” lecture delivered to female students, in which the burden of preventing harassment was implicitly placed on how they dressed. Even at the time, this felt regressive; in hindsight, it is indefensible.

What remains most disturbing, however, was the arbitrary abuse of institutional power in the final year. While I personally met attendance requirements, several peers did not “play the game” socially or politically. They did not ingratiate themselves with the programme head. As a result, they were randomly barred from sitting their third-year exams and placed into a vague, punitive “transition” period that effectively blocked completion of their degree due to the lack of attendance.

Meanwhile, other students; those with connections to “higher-ups” were quietly allowed to proceed and graduate without issue. The outcome was stark: three or four students, lacking access, influence, or resources, were forced to repeat an entire year, not due to academic failure but institutional bias. This was not administration; it was discretion weaponised.

And that is the question one is left with at the end of this programme:

For what?

What was achieved by this cruelty?
What educational standard was upheld?
What moral, academic, or institutional value justified this behaviour?

The answer appears to be: none.

This was not rigor. It was not discipline. It was not academic integrity. It was power exercised cheaply, unevenly, and without accountability; at the expense of students who trusted the institution to act in good faith.

That is the legacy of this course. And no amount of retrospective framing can make it otherwise.
